questions.stem: The Greek suffix '-phobia' means an extreme or irrational 'fear'. What exact specific fear does 'arachnophobia' logically describe?

options.option_text: The intense psychological fear of towering skyscrapers and tall buildings.
The extreme and irrational fear of spiders and other arachnids.
The deep terrifying fear of completely dark and completely unlit rooms.
The severe crippling fear of speaking loudly in front of huge crowds.

questions.explanation: 'Arachnophobia' combines 'arachne' (spider) and 'phobia' (fear). It specifically refers to an intense, irrational fear of spiders.

questions.stem: The suffix '-phobia' means 'fear'. Which of the following specific terms accurately describes the extreme fear of enclosed or totally confined physical spaces?

options.option_text: Agoraphobia___
Acrophobia____
Claustrophobia
Hydrophobia___

questions.explanation: 'Claustrophobia' comes from Latin 'claustrum' (a shut-in place) and Greek 'phobia' (fear). It is the fear of enclosed spaces, such as elevators or small rooms.

questions.stem: Combining the Greek prefix 'acro-' (highest/extremity) with the suffix '-phobia' (fear), what exact fear does 'acrophobia' represent?

options.option_text: The intense, paralyzing fear of very sharp and dangerous physical objects.
The deep, uncontrollable emotional fear of flying in commercial airplanes.
The absolute extreme fear of rapidly driving high-speed mechanical vehicles.
The extreme or completely irrational psychological fear of heights.

questions.explanation: 'Acrophobia' combines 'akron' (summit/highest point) and 'phobia' (fear). It specifically means an extreme or irrational fear of heights.

questions.stem: The suffix '-phobia' means 'fear'. What exact psychological condition does 'agoraphobia' properly and accurately describe?

options.option_text: The severe fear of places or situations that might cause panic, helplessness, or embarrassment, often public spaces.
The intense and totally irrational fear of various species of harmless agricultural farm animals.
The deep psychological fear of consuming genetically modified or chemically altered agricultural food products.
The extreme fear of looking directly into highly reflective household mirrors or shiny glass surfaces.

questions.explanation: 'Agoraphobia' originates from the Greek word 'agora' (place of assembly/marketplace). It is characterized by anxiety in situations where the sufferer perceives their environment to be unsafe with no easy way to escape.

questions.stem: The suffix '-phobia' means 'fear'. Historically and medically, 'hydrophobia' is widely known as a specific extreme fear of water, but it is also a well-known historical symptom of which deadly viral disease?

options.option_text: Cholera
Malaria
Rabies
Tetanus

questions.explanation: 'Hydrophobia' means fear of water. In historical medical terminology, it was often used as a synonym for Rabies, because people in the late stages of the disease experience painful throat spasms when attempting to swallow liquids.

questions.stem: Combining the Greek prefix 'xeno-' (stranger/foreigner) with '-phobia' (fear), what is the precise definition of 'xenophobia'?

options.option_text: The severe psychological fear of discovering extraterrestrial alien lifeforms from outer space.
The deep-rooted, irrational dislike or extreme fear of people from other countries or entirely different cultures.
The absolute paralyzing fear of highly advanced, sentient, and independent artificial intelligence systems.
The intense fear of adopting newly developed cutting-edge scientific electronic technologies.

questions.explanation: 'Xenophobia' combines 'xenos' (stranger/foreigner) and 'phobia' (fear). It denotes prejudice, dislike, or fear against people from other countries.

questions.stem: The suffix '-phobia' means 'fear'. Which of the following extremely specific terms accurately describes the severe irrational psychological fear of the night or complete darkness?

options.option_text: Photophobia_
Heliophobia_
Thermophobia
Nyctophobia_

questions.explanation: 'Nyctophobia' combines the Greek 'nyx' (night) and 'phobia' (fear). It specifically refers to an extreme or irrational fear of the night or of complete darkness.

questions.stem: The Latin root 'claustro-' means 'shut' or 'enclosed'. Combining it with '-phobia' gives 'claustrophobia'. What is the precise clinical meaning of this well-known anxiety disorder?

options.option_text: An intense, irrational fear of open or crowded public spaces
An intense, irrational fear of confined or enclosed spaces
An intense, irrational fear of heights and elevated surfaces
An intense, irrational fear of darkness and low-light settings

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'claustro-' comes from Latin 'claustrum' meaning a locked or enclosed space, so claustrophobia is the dread of confined areas such as elevators or small rooms. Option A describes agoraphobia (Greek 'agora' = marketplace/open space) — the most common distractor since both phobias involve environmental triggers rather than objects or creatures.

questions.stem: Surveys consistently rank it among humanity's top fears, outranking even death. A student freezes and goes blank every time she must address an audience from a podium. Which phobia precisely names this condition?

options.option_text: Logophobia — pathological dread of words or verbal communication
Glossophobia — pathological fear of public speaking or oral address
Phonophobia — pathological sensitivity and dread of sudden loud sounds
Eremophobia — pathological dread of silence or being in empty spaces

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'glosso-' derives from Greek 'glossa' meaning tongue — the organ of speech — so glossophobia is specifically the fear of speaking before an audience. Option A is the classic trap: logophobia (logos = word) relates to words in general and can include written words; it does not target the performance dimension of public speaking.

questions.stem: In Greek, 'pyr' (also 'pyro-') means fire. A wildfire survivor develops overwhelming panic at the sight of candles, matchsticks, and open hearths. Which phobia term precisely names this condition?

options.option_text: Thermophobia — pathological dread of heat or very high temperatures
Pyrophobia — pathological dread of fire and all sources of open flame
Photophobia — pathological intolerance of bright or intense light
Incendiophobia — pathological dread of large-scale urban fires or arson

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'pyr' (fire) + phobia = pyrophobia, the irrational dread of fire. Thermophobia (thermos = heat) is the closest distractor but pertains broadly to high temperatures, not to fire as a phenomenon. Photophobia is a genuine clinical term yet refers to light sensitivity — candidates confuse it because both fire and light involve visible energy.

questions.stem: The Greek root 'kyon/kyno-' means dog, while 'ailouros' means cat. Which pairing of phobia terms correctly maps both roots to their recognised psychological meanings?

options.option_text: Cynophobia = fear of dogs; Ailurophobia = fear of cats
Cynophobia = fear of cats; Ailurophobia = fear of dogs
Cynophobia = fear of dogs; Ailurophobia = fear of mice
Cynophobia = fear of wolves; Ailurophobia = fear of small animals

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'kyno-' (dog) gives cynophobia; 'ailouros' (cat) gives ailurophobia — both are standard specific phobias recognised in clinical literature. Option B is the classic reversal trap. Option D misreads 'kyno-' as wolf; the Greek for wolf is 'lykos', giving lycophobia, a wholly different term.

questions.stem: Three of the following phobia terms are correctly paired with their meanings. Which one is INCORRECTLY defined?

options.option_text: Nyctophobia — intense irrational dread of the dark or nighttime
Ombrophobia — intense irrational dread of rain or being rained upon
Ergophobia — intense irrational dread of work or occupational tasks
Logophobia — intense irrational dread of numbers and calculations

questions.explanation: D is the incorrect pair: 'logos' (Greek) means word or reason, so logophobia is the fear of words — not numbers. The dread of numbers is arithmophobia (arithmos = number) or numerophobia. Options A, B, and C are accurately defined: 'nyktos' = night, 'ombros' = rain shower, and 'ergon' = work — all standard phobia roots tested in competitive exams.

questions.stem: Decomposing 'triskaidekaphobia': 'treis' = three, 'kai' = and, 'deka' = ten. What exact irrational fear does this compound Greek-derived term describe?

options.option_text: Extreme dread of multi-digit numbers and long numerical sequences
Extreme dread of the number thirteen in any setting or form
Extreme dread of Fridays that happen to fall on the 13th of the month
Extreme dread of odd prime numbers appearing in everyday life

questions.explanation: B is correct: three (treis) + and (kai) + ten (deka) = thirteen, so triskaidekaphobia is the fear of the number 13 in any context whatsoever. Option C is the chief distractor — the fear specifically of Friday the 13th has its own distinct term: paraskevidekatriaphobia ('Paraskevi' = Friday in Greek). Triskaidekaphobia is broader and does not require a calendar Friday.

questions.stem: Most phobia terms are pure Greek compounds, but one well-known phobia uses a Latin-derived first component, making it a Greco-Latin hybrid. Which of the following fits that description?

options.option_text: Acrophobia — 'akros' (Greek: topmost/summit) + phobia (Greek: fear)
Claustrophobia — 'claustrum' (Latin: enclosed space) + phobia (Greek)
Xenophobia — 'xenos' (Greek: stranger/foreigner) + phobia (Greek: fear)
Hydrophobia — 'hydor' (Greek: water) + phobia (Greek: fear)

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'claustrum' derives from Latin 'claudere' (to close/shut), not from Greek, making claustrophobia a Greco-Latin hybrid. All three distractors — 'akros', 'xenos', 'hydor' — are genuine Greek roots. This distinction is tested in advanced vocabulary sections to separate rote learners from candidates who understand classical etymology.
